documents.abstract: This paper presents the results of the co-design stage of the project “Strengthening Teachers’ Digital Competences,” focused on assessment mediated by Artificial Intelligence (AI) in 12 Centros María Espínola (CME) in Uruguay. The starting point was a previous mixed-methods diagnosis (N = 187 surveys and 11 focus groups) that revealed low competence levels in the area of assessment (M = 1.88 on a 4-point scale), along with marked ethical resistance to replacing the pedagogical relationship with algorithmic processes. In February 2026, collaborative workshops were held with the participation of more than 20 teachers and CME coordinators. The co-design methodology made it possible to identify that teachers demand situated training that does not focus solely on technique, but rather on the pedagogical redesign of tasks to foster critical paraphrasing and avoid uncritical plagiarism. Likewise, ethical red lines were defined, preserving human dimensions such as empathy and the socio-emotional context as domains exclusive to teachers. The results highlight the importance of Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and the seminar effect (peer learning) as pillars for the sustainability of training in contexts of vulnerability. This collective construction helps ensure that the final proposal, structured into flexible pathways, is feasible, responsive to real classroom needs, and coherently integrated into the Ceibal ecosystem.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering mathematics classrooms, yet little is known about how teachers psychologically adapt to its use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an organizing framework and the transactional theory of stress and coping as a process account, this study examined whether general technology-related technostress statistically accounted for part of the association between cognitive flexibility and ChatGPT acceptance. Methods This cross-sectional correlational study included 127 in-service middle-school mathematics teachers from 30 public schools in the Marmara Region of Türkiye. Validated self-report instruments assessed cognitive flexibility and general technology-related technostress. ChatGPT acceptance was calculated from perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward use, and pedagogical AI self-efficacy; actual use was excluded. A regression-based indirect-effect analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples) controlled for gender. Results Cognitive flexibility was negatively associated with general technology-related technostress (B = −0.243, p < 0.001), which was negatively associated with ChatGPT acceptance (B = −0.620, p < 0.001). Cognitive flexibility was positively associated with ChatGPT acceptance after technostress was included (B = 0.355, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (B = 0.151, SE = 0.043, 95% CI [0.074, 0.241]). Discussion Teachers reporting greater cognitive flexibility also reported lower general technology-related technostress and greater ChatGPT acceptance. Because all variables were measured concurrently by self-report, the indirect effect is statistical and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. The findings identify psychological adaptation as a relevant complement to technology-centered accounts of GenAI acceptance and motivate longitudinal research with practicing teachers.

This study examines the factors shaping attitudes towards ChatGPT inclusive of personality traits, ideological orientations, AI literacy, gender, and cultural context. In Study 1 ( N total = 500; N valid = 472 Serbia), positive perceptions of ChatGPT as a learning tool and personal assistant were linked to higher AI literacy and supportive views of AI, whereas negative AI-related attitudes predicted concerns about ChatGPT’s cognitive impairment and existential threats. Gender played a crucial role: among men, higher levels of right-wing authoritarianism (RWA) and social dominance orientation (SDO) predicted more negative attitudes, while among women, RWA, SDO, and Openness were associated with more positive views. Study 2 compared German (as a representative of one of the most developed countries, especially in AI development; N total = 115; N valid = 112) and Serbian (as an example of a less AI-developed country; N total = 119; N valid = 117) samples, revealing significant differences (e.g., Germans scored higher in AI literacy, while Serbian participants scored higher in Conscientiousness and Extraversion. We further found different and unique effects of the examined predictors on participants’ AI- and ChatGPT-related attitudes across both samples, possibly driven by the above-mentioned base differences. These findings underscore a complex interplay of individual and cultural factors that drive divergent interpretations of AI’s societal role, highlighting the need to consider context when assessing public acceptance of emerging technologies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Enterprises increasingly rely on complex, cross-functional business processes spanning ERP, CRM, ticketing, and legacy systems, generating massive event logs that conventional process mining and robotic process automation (RPA) tools struggle to interpret holistically. Rule based process discovery algorithms such as Heuristic Miner and Inductive Miner produce structurally valid models but cannot explain deviations in natural language, generalize across process variants, or adapt to evolving organizational vocabularies [1], [2]. This paper proposes Cognitive Process Intelligence (CPI), a framework integrating Generative AI with automated workflow discovery to bridge this gap. We introduce ProcessGPT, a 220M-parameter domain adapted transformer continually pre-trained on enterprise event logs, BPMN repositories, and standard operating procedure (SOP) documentation, and augmented with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) over an indexed corpus of 1.8 million process artifacts. The system performs four cognitive tasks: event-log-driven process discovery, deviation and anomaly detection, natural-language-to-workflow translation, and automated process documentation generation. Evaluated on the BPI Challenge 2017/2019 logs and a proprietary 42,000-case enterprise dataset, the proposed CPI framework achieves a 0.95 average F1-score in process model discovery, reduces hallucinated process steps from 9.1% to 1.4% through RAG grounding, and operates at 96 ms average latency, substantially outperforming classical miners, sequence-to-sequence deep learning baselines, and general-purpose LLMs. Expert evaluation confirms near-human interpretability of generated workflow narratives, positioning CPI as a practical cognitive layer for enterprise automation.Originally published in Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications, Volume 33, Issue 8 (2024), pages 9173–9185. Original article: https://eudoxuspress.com/index.php/pub/article/view/5676

Background Superficial fungal infections present a growing threat to global public health. Traditional diagnostic techniques, including microscopy and culture, are time-consuming and subjective, often limiting diagnostic accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic tools offer a promising adjunct to improve efficiency and standardization of microscopic fungal detection. Methods We systematically compared six deep learning models, including the You Only Look Once (YOLO) series, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) series and the Detection Transformer (DETR). Three evaluation datasets were constructed. Datasets 1 and 2 (derived from 4000 hyphae and 4500 spore images) were used to assess image-level detection using sensitivity, precision and F1 score. Dataset 1 was manually annotated for the YOLO series and DETR; Dataset 2 (unannotated) served as the CNN series’ benchmark. Dataset 3 (1, 870 specimens from 1, 730 patients) was used to evaluate sample-level performance via confusion matrix analysis for the YOLO series and DETR models, employing medical records as the reference standard. The best-performing model was optimized and deployed into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform for real-time clinical decision support. Results YOLOv11 outperformed all other evaluated architectures. Detection was generally better at 400× than at 200× magnification. Notably, the F1 score for hyphae detection by YOLOv11 increased from 90.42% (200×) to 92.06% (400×). All models achieved higher accuracy for spores than hyphae. Patient-level confusion-matrix analysis confirmed YOLOv11 superiority. After optimizing an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.25 and the maximum confidence (Cmax) strategy, 200× hyphae F1 rose to 97.84% and the positive predictive value (PPV) to 98.27%. Subgroup analysis showed robust performance across different diseases, with tinea capitis reaching the highest F1 score (98.53%). Conclusion The optimized YOLOv11 model demonstrates potential as a rapid and standardized supportive tool for the microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections. Integration into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform demonstrates the feasibility of real-time AI-assisted fungal detection, offering a standardized tool to support clinical decision-making. This work supports AI as a potential complement to clinical and laboratory expertise, pending further validation in prospective and multi-center settings, and highlights its potential to streamline fungal infection diagnostic workflows.

Patagonia Inc. was an exemplary company blending human resource management (HRM) strategies with corporate sustainability to achieve success in building an eco-friendly culture. However, no agreement has been conceptualizing this link. Therefore, the objective of this paper was to identify the contents of its common-good HRM strategies and results. The study identified common-good HRM practices as; flexible job design, green recruitment, hiring to culture, decent pay, innovative benefits, green seminars, and humanistic management. Consequently, significant job satisfaction, commitment, and performance improvements were seen. The review also identified improved economic, innovative, green, social, and competitive dimensions of performances besides sustainability as organizational outcomes to be benchmarked. Researchers, practitioners, and policymakers may use the proposed conceptual model to empirically test its validity across different contexts and in its practical adoption.

Background/Objectives: Treatment allocation for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly complex task that requires multidisciplinary tumor board (MDT) input; however, its accessibility and reliability can vary across the healthcare system. Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential clinical decision-making tools to aid MDTs. Our aim was to compare different LLM-generated treatment recommendations for HCC cases with MDT decisions. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 100 HCC cases discussed during MDT meetings in a tertiary-care hospital in Cluj-Napoca, Romania. Identical prompts and structured clinical information were offered to four different LLMs (ChatGPT-5, a customized Tumor Board ChatGPT, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Gemini 2.5 Pro), each of which was required to provide treatment recommendations. Concordance with the MDT decisions was assessed across the first, second, and third treatment options. Inter-model differences were evaluated using Cochran’s Q and Holm-adjusted exact McNemar tests. Chance-corrected agreement was assessed using Cohen’s kappa (κ), and generalized estimating equations evaluated associations between concordance and clinical complexity. Results: First-recommendation concordance was 81% (95% CI 72.2–87.5) for GPT-5, 80% (71.1–86.7) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, 78% (68.9–85.0) for TumorBoard ChatGPT, and 63% (53.2–71.8) for Gemini 2.5 Flash; cumulative top-3 concordance reached 95%, 92%, 95%, and 86%, respectively. GPT-5 (κ = 0.754) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (κ = 0.743) showed substantial chance-corrected agreement. Gemini 2.5 Flash showed significantly lower concordance, including after adjustment for BCLC stage, Child–Pugh class, tumor burden, and treatment category (p = 0.006), while these clinical complexity variables were not significantly associated with concordance. Conclusions: LLMs showed moderate-to-substantial agreement with MDT decisions, with meaningful inter-model differences, for a complex disease, such as HCC. Our study highlights that, while the need for human oversight is essential, LLMs could serve as supportive tools for expert guidance in some clinical settings and underscore AI’s potential in enhancing liver cancer care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming computer‐assisted learning, yet little is known about how students of colour engage with AI within authentic educational settings. Existing research has focused primarily on academic integrity, efficiency and technological adoption, with comparatively less attention to students' own experiences of AI‐mediated learning. Objectives This study examined how students of colour in online apprenticeship programs constructed narratives of agency, recognition and negotiation while engaging with generative AI and what these experiences reveal about AI‐mediated learning within apprenticeship education. Methods A qualitative narrative inquiry was conducted over 9 months with five secondary school apprentices participating in online placements across healthcare, government, finance, technology and public service. Data comprised repeated narrative interviews, classroom observations, digital artifacts and field notes, which were analyzed using manual narrative coding. Results Three interconnected patterns emerged. First, students exercised agency by strategically using, refusing, verifying, revising and disclosing AI in ways that maintained authorship and credibility. Second, participants viewed AI as procedurally fair while also recognizing that generic responses often overlooked their cultural and linguistic identities. Third, students negotiated tensions between AI‐generated outputs and institutional expectations through continual verification and adaptation, while proposing design features that would better support transparency, learning and equitable participation. Conclusions The findings suggest that effective AI‐mediated learning extends beyond technical proficiency to include learners' capacity to exercise agency, establish legitimate authorship and experience meaningful recognition within educational contexts. The study introduces Institutional AI Literacy and Recognition Bandwidth as interpretive concepts for understanding how students of colour navigate AI within apprenticeship learning and highlights the importance of designing AI systems that support transparent, equitable and culturally responsive learning experiences.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background Cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have accelerated the global development of AI-driven mHealth apps, offering diverse functionalities to support personal health management. While China’s AI health industry has expanded rapidly within a collectivist cultural context, limited empirical attention has been given to how specific AI features are associated with users’ continued use of these apps, particularly among young adults. Objective Guided by the Expectation Confirmation Model and extended AI-related features, this study examined the factors associated with continuance intention toward AI-driven mHealth apps among young Chinese adults aged 18–34. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted, collecting data from 319 valid respondents. Data were analyzed using SPSS 29.0 and Jamovi 2.6.24 to evaluate direct, mediation, and serial mediation associations among the constructs. Results The findings demonstrate that satisfaction statistically bridged the indirect associations between core ECM constructs (expectation confirmation and perceived performance) and continuance intention, as well as between AI quality and continuance intention. Furthermore, bootstrapping analysis supported a sequential mediation pathway, showing that expectation confirmation was indirectly associated with continuance intention through the proposed sequential pathway of perceived performance and satisfaction. Conclusion The findings suggest that developers should consider the technical reliability and performance of AI-driven health management and monitoring functions to better align with user needs. Moreover, collaboration between health experts and industry practitioners may support the development of content for AI-driven mHealth adoption.

Conversational AI is used for sustained and nighttime interaction, raising questions about associated psychological risks. Guided by the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this cross-sectional study examined AI interaction and hypomanic persistence tendency among young adults screening positive for hypomanic risk. Interaction intensity and nighttime involvement served as stimuli; emotional contagion, emotion regulation difficulties, and sleep rhythm disturbance as organism-level variables; and hypomanic persistence tendency as the response. Partial least squares structural equation modeling estimated direct and indirect associations, including sequential paths; necessary condition analysis assessed bottlenecks. Both AI-use variables showed positive associations with hypomanic persistence tendency, stronger for nighttime involvement. Significant indirect associations were observed through the three organism-level variables. Emotional contagion showed a moderate necessity effect, while emotion regulation difficulties and sleep rhythm disturbance showed stronger bottleneck characteristics; neither AI-use variable was necessary. These findings extend research to naturally occurring engagement and distinguish association-based importance from necessity.

This project examines how the presentation of human–AI collaboration, scientific uncertainty, and supporting explanations shapes public acceptance of AI chatbots for health misinformation correction. Guided by the Human–AI Interaction framework grounded in the Theory of Interactive Media Effects (HAII–TIME), the study investigates whether these features independently and jointly influence trust in a chatbot, attitudes toward using it to correct health misinformation, and intentions to use it for this purpose. The study employed a 3 × 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with a final analytical sample of 424 participants in China. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 12 conditions and viewed a simulated chatbot conversation addressing the false claim that insulin injections are addictive. Human–AI collaboration was described as human-dominated, with experts leading the evaluation and AI assisting; AI-dominated, with AI leading and experts verifying; or AI-only, without human involvement. Correction uncertainty varied according to whether the accompanying notice described the scientific evidence as broadly consistent or unresolved. Correction transparency varied according to whether the chatbot disclosed supporting reasons and sources. Analyses examined the main and interaction effects of these features while accounting for demographic characteristics, AI literacy, eHealth literacy, and perceived risks of AI hallucinations.

documents.abstract: Road accidents remain a critical public safety issue, where detection often depends on witnesses calling authorities, leading to delays of several minutes before police and ambulances are dispatched. This study presents CrashSenseAI (CSAI), an Edge artificial intelligence (Edge AI) accident detection and notification system built on You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) and YOLOv12 models. Using a labeled dataset of accident and non-accident images, we trained Nano, Small, and Medium variants with batch sizes of 16 and 32 to evaluate accuracy–latency trade-offs. Results show YOLOv12n achieved the lowest inference latency (3.6–3.7 ms) with high precision (0.89), while YOLOv8s provided the best balance of accuracy and efficiency (Recall 0.85, Precision 0.90, mean average precision (mAP) at an Intersection over Union threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5 = 0.89) and mAP@0.5–0.95 = 0.70) at 4.8–5.0 ms. Larger variants improved mAP@0.5 scores (up to 0.90) but incurred higher latency (11–14 ms). CSAI captures timestamped frames with latitude and longitude, automatically notifying police, ambulances, and nearby hospitals to speed response and scene clearance, reduce traffic congestion, and improve victim survival during the golden hour. By combining real-time detection, geolocation, evidence generation, and automated alerting, CSAI demonstrates practical scalability for AI-driven intelligent transportation and road safety applications.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: Abstract Pediatric and adult cancers diverge profoundly in their molecular architecture, yet whether these differences extend to genome-scale genetic dependencies remains poorly characterized, with prior studies examining single subtypes or individual algorithms rather than a systematic, interpretable comparison. To address this gap, we tested whether Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 loss-of-function dependency profiles can discriminate pediatric from adult cancer cell lines, and applied explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the genes driving this distinction. Chronos-normalized CRISPR GeneEffect scores for 18,531 genes across 1208 cell lines (242 pediatric, 966 adult) were analyzed; class imbalance was corrected with the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) within each training fold, differentially dependent genes were identified by Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction, and 200 features were retained by SelectKBest. Eleven classifiers were benchmarked under 5-fold cross-validation across 11 metrics, and predictions were interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) In this first (to our knowledge) genome-scale, multi-classifier comparison Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) achieved the best discrimination (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve [ROC-AUC] = 0.909, accuracy = 88.7%, Matthews Correlation Coefficient [MCC] = 0.632, Brier score = 0.089), with the leading ensemble and margin-based models reaching ROC-AUC values near 0.90. Among 3602 differentially dependent genes (FDR < 0.05), Integrin-Linked Kinase (ILK), Talin-1 (TLN1), and Aurora Kinase A (AURKA) showed greater dependency in pediatric lines, whereas Glutathione Peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and Insulin-like Growth Factor 2 messenger RNA-Binding Protein 1 (IGF2BP1) were comparatively more essential in adult lines. SHAP highlighted CHMP4B, IGF2BP1, GPX4, and LDB1, and the representative true-positive LIME case emphasized IGF2BP1, PAQR6, and CDS2. By exposing dependencies that adult-centric precision-oncology programs overlook, this work provides a framework for age-specific target discovery and prioritizes the pediatric-enriched ILK–TLN1 mechanotransduction axis for experimental validation.

Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare poses significant challenges for evaluation due to algorithmic complexity and evolving performance. Existing evidence generation guidelines, primarily designed for static medical technologies, may inadequately address the unique characteristics of generative AI. Here, we conducted a comparative analysis of evidence generation guidelines from six countries, examining recommendations for efficacy and effectiveness evaluations, health economic evaluations, social and equity evaluations, and uncertainty management for AI technologies. Across 56 documents, we found a consistent preference for randomised controlled trials and cost-effectiveness analyses, alongside emerging acceptance of alternative study designs and real-world evidence to accommodate the evolving nature of AI technologies. However, current frameworks lack specific guidance for the stochastic, non-deterministic, and adaptive learning properties of generative AI technologies. Moving forward, evidence generation guidelines require methodological and conceptual adaptations in order to improve the value assessment for generative AI technologies.
topics: Health Systems, Economic Evaluations, Quality of Life
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Surface ligand-modified nanoparticles (SMNPs), which immobilize surface ligands on nanoscale scaffolds, represent important nanomaterials for diverse applications. While surface ligands critically dictate the functions of SMNPs, their systematic discovery remains elusive. The major challenge in using artificial intelligence to predict and screen effective surface ligands and SMNPs across extensive chemical space is the scarcity of high-quality, standardized data sets. This impedes SMNP nanotechnology and leaves an enormous functional landscape largely unmapped. For antibacterial gold nanoparticles, available surface-ligand data sets are extremely sparse (<102), whereas public small-molecule libraries exceed 1010 entries. Here, we introduce a cross-scale (from small molecules to nanoparticles) transfer-cascade learning framework, called TRADE, that transforms the structural–activity patterns of molecular antibiotics into predictive principles for the surface ligands of nanoparticle antibiotics. Within TRADE, we chemically deconstruct molecular antibiotics into conserved scaffolds and variable substituents for transfer learning and combine a multitier, coarse-to-fine cascade to narrow the search space. We identify a new class of 24 surface ligands with high predicted antibacterial efficacy for decorating gold nanoparticles across over 9 million molecules. The leading auricidin inhibits bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis and demonstrates potent antimicrobial activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium, with minimum inhibitory concentrations as low as 0.5–1 μg/mL. Across multiple animal infection models, auricidin exhibits exceptional therapeutic efficacy and robustness, superior to vancomycin, minimal toxicity, and low susceptibility to resistance evolution. This work proposes an intelligent strategy for discovering new functional nanoscale entities by integrating cross-domain transfer and cascade learning.

Machine Learning Services help enterprises turn data into actionable intelligence through predictive models, intelligent automation, personalization, and real-time decision-making. From ML consulting and custom model development to MLOps, deployment, and optimization, these services support the complete machine learning lifecycle.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Customer retention has become increasingly important for organizations operating in highly competitive service industries. In the local non-alcoholic beverage sector, businesses continuously seek strategies that can strengthen customer relationships and encourage long-term patronage. Despite the recognized importance of customer satisfaction and customer engagement, limited studies have examined how these variables collectively influence customer retention within local beverage enterprises. Guided by Expectancy Disconfirmation Theory, the Consumers' Online Brand-Related Activities Framework, and Service-Profit Chain Theory, this study examined customer satisfaction, customer engagement, and customer retention intent among customers of selected local non-alcoholic beverage chains in Valenzuela City. The study further investigated demographic differences, examined the relationships among the variables, evaluated the mediating role of customer engagement, and developed a Customer Engagement-Satisfaction-Retention Framework. Findings revealed that respondents generally demonstrated favorable levels of customer engagement, customer satisfaction, and customer retention intent. Product quality emerged as the most influential component of customer satisfaction, while cognitive engagement was the strongest dimension of customer engagement. The results further showed that customer satisfaction significantly influences customer engagement and customer retention intent. Customer engagement likewise significantly affects customer retention intent and serves as an important mechanism through which satisfaction translates into stronger retention-related behaviors. The proposed Customer Engagement-Satisfaction-Retention Framework highlights the importance of integrating service excellence, customer engagement initiatives, and customer satisfaction strategies to achieve sustainable customer loyalty and long-term business success. The findings contribute to customer relationship management literature and provide practical insights for local beverage enterprises seeking to improve competitiveness and customer retention.

Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a pivotal advancement in textile systems, integrating intelligent sensing, wearable computing, IoT, and machine learning applications on smart fabrics for real-time monitoring of object behavior through predictive analytics. The primary areas of application identified in the investigation include healthcare, industrial safety, sports and fitness. Emerging domains represent; AI-enhanced wearable fabrics are perpetually evolving for ongoing patient surveillance and preventive health measures. The most significant security risk identified during this analysis is data breaches, closely followed by limited system access, adversarial AI assaults and denial of service attacks. Privacy-preserving technologies have emerged as a significant domain, with encryption along with blockchain, edge computing, and federated learning. This meta-analysis offers insights regarding contemporary research trends and obstacles in cybersecurity which will assist researchers in creating secure and sustainable AI-integrated wearable textile systems.

Digital supply chains face cybersecurity threats from interconnectedness and IoT devices. Real-time tracking increases risks in cyber-physical systems with vulnerable endpoints. Blockchain-IoT integration creates vulnerabilities through weak security protocols. Risk frameworks like ISO 31000 and NIST SP 800-30 guide risk identification and treatment. AI enables anomaly detection, while blockchain provides immutable records. Regulatory compliance with CCPA, GDPR, and ISO 28000 ensures data privacy. Industry 5.0 emphasizes human-AI collaboration for resilience. Future developments include AI analytics and IoT security through lightweight cryptography. Integrating cybersecurity with sustainability will support resilient supply chains. Multidisciplinary collaboration and adaptive governance address risks in value-driven networks.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: This project contains the de-identified data and supporting documentation for the study “How Should AI Voice Guides Explain Paintings? An Experimental Study of Guidance Strategy and Voice Persona Using Chinese Landscape Paintings.” The study used a Unity-based virtual gallery featuring six Chinese landscape paintings. A 3 × 2 within-subjects experiment with 21 university students compared three guidance strategies—Minimal Prompt, Standard Introduction, and Active Inquiry—and two voice personas—Warm Young Female Guide and Calm Senior Male Guide. The outcomes included user engagement, subjective task load, human–AI trust, and immediate knowledge retention. The shared files include participant-level observations across the experimental conditions, variable definitions, scoring procedures, and documentation of missing or invalid knowledge-test records. These materials support the reproduction of the statistical analyses, tables, and figures reported in the manuscript. Participants are represented by anonymous identifiers, and directly identifying information is excluded.

As claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI) and artificial general intelligence (AGI) proliferate, we ask a simple question: do frontier AI models have a sense of data, i.e., can they reliably select the right data for training? We introduce DataSense-Bench to study this capability through the fundamental problem of data selection and performance forecasting in machine learning. We ask AI agents to select and rank candidate training subsets that can be used to fine-tune a small LLM model. Agents are allowed to inspect the data, write and execute analysis code, and run model forward passes, but can not train the model or access the actual evaluation tasks. We then fine-tune the base model on each selected subset and evaluate its post-training performance under a standardized protocol. We instantiate the benchmark in terminal problem solving and tool use, selecting trajectories from OpenThoughts-Agent and EnvScaler and evaluating on TBLite and BFCL, respectively. We then evaluate the agents along two complementary dimensions: the post-training performance of the top-ranked subset, reflecting the ability to identify high-value training data, and ranking accuracy, reflecting the ability to predict the relative performance of the selected subsets. In our experiments, selection gains over random selection are limited; agents do not reliably rank their selected groups, and ranking ability does not hold consistently across tasks: Astra identifies the best group in all three tool-use runs but in only one of three terminal runs. Analysis of execution traces on both tasks shows that agents often use similar data signals while interpreting their training value differently.

Data video is a media form that integrates data visualization with video narrative, widely adopted in news reporting and business analysis. Compared with general video understanding, data video understanding places greater emphasis on accurately reading data from animated charts, integrating evidence across charts and time, and understanding how narrative organization and visual design communicate information. Yet existing benchmarks target either general videos or static charts, and data video understanding has not been systematically evaluated. We present DataVista, the first benchmark for data video understanding, containing 961 real-world data videos and 6,775 evaluation questions organized under a three-level progressive capability framework (data perception, temporal reasoning, narrative understanding) with 10 fine-grained question types across five topic domains. Systematic evaluation of 19 mainstream MLLMs shows that the best-performing model, Gemini-3.1-Pro, achieves 70.0% overall accuracy, still far below human expert performance, with models performing worst on Causal Reasoning and Narrative Structure. Increasing frame counts and adding subtitles mainly benefit data perception and temporal reasoning, with limited gains in narrative understanding. Further analysis of model responses identifies typical failure modes in chart reading, evidence judgment, and instruction understanding. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DataVista.

This chapter examines decentralized education ecosystems by integrating blockchain, artificial intelligence, and the metaverse for next-generation learning. It explains how blockchain can provide trust, secure credentials, learner-owned records, and verifiable micro-certifications, while AI supports personalization, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, analytics, and competency-based assessment. The metaverse adds immersive classrooms, simulations, digital campuses, and experiential skill development. The chapter argues that these technologies can transform education from institution-centered systems to learner-centered, portable, flexible, and lifelong learning ecosystems. It also discusses challenges such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, credential fraud, platform control, metaverse safety, and quality assurance.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents with little human oversight, so potential mistakes they make can go unnoticed. Users then depend on the model to report what went wrong. An honest model discloses its mistakes, while a deceptive one conceals them. However, it is unclear how current LLMs behave in such situations. In this study, we prefill LLM trajectories with synthetic mistakes. The trajectories resemble real deployments in chat and agentic settings. Models fail to disclose their mistake in 36.4% of chat and 67.1% of agentic rollouts. In 2.4% and 5.3% of rollouts, respectively, they are aware of the mistake in their chain of thought but still deceptively conceal it. Rates vary by model: for instance, Gemini 3.5 Flash knowingly conceals mistakes in up to 19.9% of agentic rollouts. In 11.9% of chat and 51.8% of agentic rollouts, models show no awareness of mistakes, even though they reliably spot them when reviewing the same transcript as an outside observer. Our results show that, as agents take on more tasks with less oversight, users cannot rely on them to self-report possible mistakes. Developers should instead use independent monitors that review agent trajectories, or specifically train models to check their past actions and disclose what they find.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The modern workplace is an intricate emotional ecosystem where human behavior, psychological well-being, and professional performance are deeply intertwined. This chapter explores the transformative convergence of artificial intelligence and emotional intelligence as a comprehensive framework for understanding, predicting, and supporting human behavior across professional contexts. Artificial intelligence is examined as an external cognitive companion that augments human decision-making and extends the practical reach of emotional intelligence into environments where direct human intervention is limited. Through natural language processing and computer vision, AI systems decode the emotional signals embedded in language, facial expression, and behavioral patterns, enabling meaningful prediction of workforce dynamics. Emotional intelligence is explored across three applied pillars — emotional appraisal, self-regulation, and purposeful emotional utilization — each carrying direct implications for leadership, collaboration, and organizational health.

The current high rate of adoption of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has led to a sense of urgency in the need to come up with immediate faculty-level literacy development. The idea of prompt literacy described in this chapter is a conceptual extension of AI literacy, focusing on the skill of developing effective prompts to achieve meaningful results in teaching, learning and assessment. It explores the current gaps in faculty preparedness and points to the absence of systematic institutional strategies to promote this new competency. The chapter also suggests faculty developmental strategies that are based on experiential learning, ethical awareness and continuous skill improvement. It also gives a detailed institutional framework to inform the systematic incorporation of prompt literacy into the faculty development programs. The chapter, with its focus on pedagogical and organizational aspects, will also help create a sustainable, responsible and context-sensitive implementation of AI in higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: RDMA can reduce communication overhead in distributed machine learning systems, but realizing these benefits in production requires more than replacing TCP. Variable-size messages, concurrent connections, bursty incasts, and service failures introduce challenges that hardware offload alone cannot address. This paper reports our experience deploying ByteExpress, a software communication layer over hardware RDMA, in ByteDance's parameter-server-based inference and training systems. We present three lessons from the deployment: efficient RDMA requires buffer management across application and transport layers; scalable communication requires coordinated management of connections, receive capacity, and outstanding data; and service availability requires recovery above the transport layer. ByteExpress combines an RDMA-aware allocator, zero-copy transfers, QP multiplexing, receive-credit flow control, a software send window, and RPC-assisted recovery. In production inference, ByteExpress reduces mean and P99 model parameter fetch latency by 35.7% and 43.7%, respectively, and total CPU usage by 10.69% compared with kernel TCP. In training, ByteExpress reduces P99 model parameter push latency by up to 74.0% compared with TCP, with no PFC pauses observed at runtime.

As leading LLMs improve on capability evaluations, their limitations in producing creative outputs on design tasks remain insufficiently characterised. Our work introduces Design Creativity Bench, a benchmark that evaluates diversity and appropriateness in UI designs. It measures distinctiveness among models on the same prompt (originality), how much a model's designs change between two prompts for the same UI goal in different product domains (creative range), and the share of a brief's acceptance criteria each design meets (appropriateness). Originality is 0.592 for same-prompt design pairs from different models (95% CI [0.582, 0.602]), far below the 0.764 for same-prompt human-model pairs (95% CI [0.751, 0.778]). Creative range is 0.581 across models (95% CI [0.567, 0.597]), against 0.902 for human designs (95% CI [0.884, 0.919]). Appropriateness is above 90% for every model, and the best model reaches 99.2%, slightly above the 98.0% for human designs. Our work shows that the default output of LLMs, though generally appropriate, is substantially more repetitive than the human baseline. This calls for strong measures to address the issue.

Healthcare monitoring is an important area where technology can significantly improve the quality, accessibility, and efficiency of medical services. Traditional healthcare systems mainly depend on periodic hospital visits and manual monitoring of patients, which may not provide continuous information about a patient's health condition. The combination of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) provides an effective solution for continuous and intelligent healthcare monitoring. In an AI-based smart healthcare monitoring system, IoT sensors are used to collect real-time physiological information such as heart rate, body temperature, blood oxygen saturation, blood pressure, and other health-related parameters. The collected data is transmitted through an IoT communication network to a cloud or processing platform. AI and machine learning techniques can then analyze the collected data, identify abnormal patterns, and support early detection of potential health problems. The proposed system provides continuous monitoring, automatic data analysis, alerts, and remote access to health information. This reduces the need for frequent manual observation and helps healthcare professionals make informed decisions based on real-time patient information. The system can be particularly useful for elderly people, patients requiring continuous observation, individuals with chronic health conditions, and remote healthcare environments. The integration of AI, IoT sensors, cloud computing, and mobile applications creates a smart healthcare environment that improves monitoring efficiency and supports timely medical intervention

Abstract With the advancement and maturing levels of related technologies, virtual reality (VR) is finding more uses in the industry, especially as a one-of-a-kind high-value generating system, and even for the general mass (e.g., entertainment and social activities). As such, there is an increasing concern for security for VR (as would be needed for any information system), which has seen only limited attention. One such area is the authentication procedures for VR users. One natural solution is to adopt the CAPTCHA as widely used in the 2D-based systems. However, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have exposed critical vulnerabilities.Furthermore, conventional 2D CAPTCHA systems may be ill-suited for immersive 3D environments, often causing interaction inconvenience, disrupting user experience, and reducing immersion. On the other hand, there may be an opportunity for drastically improving the level of security by incorporating 3D spatial reasoning and interaction, which is generally regarded as more difficult for AI to crack, into the CAPTCHA authentication procedure in VR.In this paper, we propose ''Cognitive 3D Immersive CAPTCHA'' that leverages spatial interaction and user behaviors unique to virtual environments.As a foundation for this new approach, we set forth ten design principles tailored to CAPTCHA systems in VR. To explore and validate these principles, we design four prototype CAPTCHA systems as illustrative examples.The prototypes are evaluated to assess how well each satisfies the proposed principles, through a user study, expert review, and robustness analysis.The findings support the potential of these systems, while also identifying certain vulnerabilities and suggesting directions for improvement.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is now part of everyday academic work in higher education, including feedback. However, AI feedback does not automatically lead to learning. It can help students rethink a concept, improve a draft, and notice gaps in their work, but it can also create a false sense of progress when students accept suggestions without understanding them. This Perspective article argues that responsible AI feedback depends on faculty readiness and students’ evaluative judgement. Readiness is not mainly technical. It involves pedagogical judgement: knowing how to design tasks in which students work with feedback, compare it with evidence, revise with purpose, explain their choices, and remain responsible for the final submission. The article focuses on generative AI feedback and uses metacognitive calibration as a central concept. Calibration refers to the relationship between students’ confidence or self-judgement and independently evaluated evidence of performance. Evaluative judgement concerns students’ capacity to judge the quality and relevance of feedback and work, whereas calibration concerns the accuracy of their judgements relative to independently evaluated performance evidence. The article shows how ideas from feedback literacy, evaluative judgement, and self-regulated learning need to be adapted when feedback comes from systems whose accuracy and educational value cannot be assumed. It proposes a conceptual responsible AI feedback design cycle linked to assessment integrity, university policy, and faculty development. Although the cycle requires empirical testing, it offers a practical way to support reflection, calibrated judgement, and accountability without replacing students’ thinking.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study examines how information source type, information accuracy, information type, and presentation modality shape perceived source credibility in generative AI settings. A four-way factorial experiment (N = 960) revealed that information accuracy was the dominant determinant of source credibility, while source type (human, AI) and presentation modality (text, video) produced no significant effects. The credibility penalty for factual inaccuracy was nearly four times larger than the penalty for counter-attitudinal opinion content, consistent with Expectancy Violations Theory: higher baseline accuracy expectations in verifiable domains amplify the credibility penalty for error. A significant three-way interaction further showed that human sources incurred larger penalties for factual errors than AI sources, suggesting that individuals apply unequal accuracy standards depending on source identity. The credibility consequences of accuracy violations are thus context-dependent, varying by information type and source identity. These findings offer theoretical and practical insights for AI literacy education and generative AI design.
